group.passage:
A single extra zero can turn a debt of ten coins into a debt of a hundred. That simple fact helps explain why one of the most useful ideas in mathematics was once treated with suspicion.
Zero actually does two different jobs. As a placeholder, it keeps other digits in their proper positions, so that 2106 is not confused with 216. As a number, it can be added, subtracted, and multiplied like any other. The first job appeared long before the second. The Babylonians, who counted in sixties, used a place-value system for over 1,000 years with no mark at all for an empty place, leaving readers to work out the meaning from context. By around 400 BC, scribes were pressing two small wedges into their clay tablets to fill the gap, but only between digits, never at the end of a number.
Treating zero as a number in its own right came later, in India. In 628, the astronomer Brahmagupta set out rules for it: zero is what remains when a number is taken away from itself, adding zero changes nothing, and anything multiplied by zero becomes zero. Not every rule held up, however. He declared that zero divided by zero equals zero, which mathematicians today reject.
These ideas traveled west through Arab scholars and eventually reached a young Italian named Leonardo of Pisa, now known as Fibonacci. His father worked for Italian merchants in a North African port, and it was there that the boy learned the Indian numerals. In 1202 he completed Liber Abaci, a book that showed Europeans how to use them, filled with practical problems about prices, profits, and changing one currency into another. Even so, Fibonacci called 0 a “sign,” while he described the digits one to nine as numbers.
Merchants did not rush to adopt the new system. In 1299, the leaders of Florence, a city famous for its banks, banned the new numerals, including zero. A common explanation is that they feared fraud: with a stroke of the pen, 10 could become 100, a trick that was harder to play with Roman numerals. Yet calculating with Roman numerals was slow and clumsy, and over more than a century the new digits won out. By the fifteenth century they were widely accepted, and zero had finally earned its place.

options.A: How Brahmagupta’s rules for zero became the basis of today’s arithmetic.
options.B: How zero grew into a full number and was only slowly accepted in Europe.
options.C: How Italian merchants used new numerals to build the first banks in Europe.
options.D: Why ancient peoples needed a mark to show that a place was empty.

options.B: How did the Babylonians record numbers before they used clay tablets?
options.C: When did Fibonacci begin writing Liber Abaci?

options.B: Bankers getting wrong answers by dividing numbers by zero.
options.C: Foreign traders being unable to read Roman numerals.
options.D: Young merchants finding Fibonacci’s book too hard to follow.

questions.stem: What does Fibonacci’s choice to call 0 a “sign” suggest?

options.A: He believed zero was more important than the other digits.
options.B: He did not understand how to calculate with the new numerals.
options.C: Even he did not yet regard zero as a true number like one to nine.
options.D: He wanted to hide the fact that the symbol had come from India.

translation_zh.text:
多寫一個零，就能把十枚錢幣的債變成一百枚。這個簡單的事實，有助於說明為什麼數學裡最有用的概念之一，曾經被人用懷疑的眼光看待。
零其實有兩種不同的工作。作為占位符號，它讓其他數字留在正確的位置上，所以 2106 不會和 216 搞混。作為一個數，它可以和其他數一樣拿來加、減、乘。第一種用途出現的時間遠早於第二種。以六十進位計數的巴比倫人，使用位值制長達一千多年，卻完全沒有表示空位的記號，讀的人得從上下文推敲數字的意思。到了大約西元前 400 年，書記會在泥板上壓出兩個小楔形符號來填補空位，但只用在數字之間，從不用在數字的末尾。
把零當成一個獨立的數，是後來在印度才出現的。西元 628 年，天文學家婆羅摩笈多為零訂出規則：一個數減去自己，剩下的就是零；加上零，數不會改變；任何數乘以零都變成零。不過，並不是每條規則都站得住腳。他宣稱零除以零等於零，今天的數學家並不接受。
這些概念經由阿拉伯學者向西傳播，最後傳到一位名叫比薩的李奧納多、今天人稱費波那契的義大利年輕人手上。他的父親在北非一個港口為義大利商人工作，他就是在那裡學會印度數字的。1202 年，他完成了《計算之書》，教歐洲人如何使用這些數字，書中滿是關於價格、利潤和貨幣兌換的實用問題。即使如此，費波那契仍把 0 稱為「符號」，而把一到九稱為「數字」。
商人們並沒有急著採用這套新系統。1299 年，以銀行業聞名的佛羅倫斯，其領導者禁止使用包括零在內的新數字。常見的解釋是他們害怕詐欺：筆一揮，10 就能變成 100，而用羅馬數字就比較難動這種手腳。然而，用羅馬數字計算又慢又笨拙，經過一百多年，新數字終於勝出。到了十五世紀，它們已被廣泛接受，零也終於贏得了自己的地位。

open_tasks.prompt: In 2–3 English sentences, explain the two different jobs that zero does and why some people in Europe did not trust it at first.
reference_answers: Zero works as a placeholder that keeps other digits in the right positions, and it is also a number that can be used in calculations. Some Europeans did not trust it because an added zero could easily make a written amount larger, so Florence banned the new numerals for a time.

有沒有說明歐洲人不信任的原因（容易造假）
有沒有用自己的話改寫，而不是照抄原文
